rows.stem: An ammeter and a voltmeter are connected in series to a battery. Their readings are noted as 'A' and 'V' respectively. If a resistor is connected in parallel with the voltmeter, then

options.label: A
options.text: A will increase, V will decrease.

options.label: B
options.text: A will decrease, V will increase.

options.label: C
options.text: Both A and V will decrease.

options.label: D
options.text: Both A and V will increase.

rows.solution:
**The answer is (A): A will increase, V will decrease.**

**Picture the circuit first.** An ammeter and a voltmeter **in series** is an unusual arrangement, and recognising why is most of the question. A voltmeter has a very **large** resistance \(R_V\); an ammeter has a very **small** one. In series, the voltmeter therefore dominates completely:

\(A = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R_A + R_V + r} \approx \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R_V}\)

and the voltmeter reads the potential difference across **itself**.

**Now connect \(R\) in parallel with the voltmeter.**

**The resistance in that part of the circuit FALLS.** A parallel combination is always smaller than either branch:

\(R_{\text{eff}} = \dfrac{R_VR}{R_V + R} < R_V\)

**Effect on the ammeter.** Total circuit resistance is now lower, so the current rises:

\(A' = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R_A + R_{\text{eff}} + r} \;>\; A \qquad \textbf{A increases.}\)

**Effect on the voltmeter.** The voltmeter reads the drop across the parallel combination, which is the emf shared out in proportion to resistance:

\(V' = \varepsilon\cdot\dfrac{R_{\text{eff}}}{R_A + R_{\text{eff}} + r}\)

Since \(R_{\text{eff}} < R_V\), that share is **smaller** than before. \(\ \textbf{V decreases.}\)

**Why they move in OPPOSITE directions**, which is what the four options are really testing. It is tempting to reason "more current, so more voltage" from \(V = IR\) — but the \(R\) in that equation has changed too, and it has fallen by more than the current has risen. The product \(I \times R_{\text{eff}}\) therefore goes down.

**A limiting case makes it obvious.** Let \(R \to 0\), a dead short across the voltmeter. Then \(R_{\text{eff}} \to 0\): the ammeter reads the largest current the circuit can give, and the voltmeter reads **zero**. That is (A) taken to its extreme, and it rules out the three alternatives at a glance.

**The practical moral.** This is precisely why a voltmeter must have a **high** resistance. Connecting one across a component is connecting a resistor in parallel with it — exactly the change made here — and it lowers the very voltage the instrument is trying to measure. The higher \(R_V\), the smaller that disturbance.

rows.subtopic: AC Voltage Applied to an Inductor and a Capacitor
rows.stem: An ac voltage is applied across an ideal inductor. The current in it
rows.solution:
**The answer is (B): the current lags the voltage by \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) cycle.**

**Derive it rather than recall it.** For an ideal inductor the applied voltage is entirely the back-emf:

\(v = L\dfrac{di}{dt}\)

With \(v = v_0\sin\omega t\):

\(\dfrac{di}{dt} = \dfrac{v_0}{L}\sin\omega t\)

Integrating:

\(i = -\dfrac{v_0}{\omega L}\cos\omega t = \dfrac{v_0}{\omega L}\sin\left(\omega t - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\)

**The current's phase is \(\pi/2\) BEHIND the voltage's**, and \(\pi/2\) is a quarter of the full \(2\pi\) cycle:

\(\boxed{\ \text{current lags voltage by } \dfrac{\pi}{2} = \dfrac{1}{4}\ \text{cycle}\ }\)

**Why it lags, physically.** An inductor opposes any **change** in current. When the driving voltage is at its peak the current is still climbing through zero; the current cannot respond instantly, so it trails behind. The inductor's opposition is to the rate of change, not to the current itself, which is why the lag is exactly a quarter cycle and not some intermediate amount.

**Telling the two halves of the option set apart.**

*Lead or lag?* An **inductor** makes the current lag; a **capacitor** makes it lead. The standard mnemonic is **CIVIL** — in a **C**apacitor, **I** comes before **V**; **V** comes before **I** in an **L**. The two options offering "leads" are the capacitor's answer.

*A quarter or a half?* A half-cycle shift, \(\pi\), would mean the current simply **reverses sign** relative to the voltage — that is what a negative resistance would do, and no passive element behaves that way. The \(\pi/2\) comes from integrating a sine into a cosine, and no other value can arise from a pure \(L\) or \(C\).

**Two consequences worth keeping.** The peak current is \(v_0/\omega L\), so the reactance \(X_L = \omega L\) grows with frequency — an inductor passes DC freely and chokes high frequencies. And because the phase difference is exactly \(90^\circ\), the power factor \(\cos\phi\) is **zero**: an ideal inductor dissipates no energy, merely storing it in its magnetic field for a quarter cycle and returning it in the next.

rows.stem: An iron needle is kept near a strong bar magnet. It will experience

options.label: A
options.text: a force of attraction and no torque.

options.label: B
options.text: a force of attraction and a torque.

options.label: D
options.text: neither a force nor a torque.

rows.solution:
**The answer is (B): a force of attraction AND a torque.**

**Two things happen, one after the other.**

**First, the needle becomes a magnet.** Iron is **ferromagnetic**, so in the bar magnet's field its domains align and it acquires an induced magnetic moment \(\vec{m}\), pointing **along** the local field.

**Then, being a dipole in a field, it experiences both effects:**

**A torque**, which is what aligns it:

\(\vec{\tau} = \vec{m}\times\vec{B}\)

Unless the needle happens to be lying exactly along the field already, \(\vec{m}\) and \(\vec{B}\) are at an angle and the torque is non-zero. This is why a compass needle swings round.

**A force**, because the field is **NON-UNIFORM**:

\(F = m\dfrac{dB}{dx}\)

A bar magnet's field is strongest at its poles and weakens with distance, so \(dB/dx \ne 0\) and there is a net force. Because the induced moment always aligns **with** the field, the force is always towards the **stronger** field — that is, **towards the magnet**. Hence attraction.

**The non-uniformity is the hinge of the question.** In a **uniform** field the two forces on the dipole's ends are equal and opposite, cancelling exactly, and only a torque survives — that is option (C), and it is the standard textbook case that makes (C) so tempting. But a real bar magnet produces nothing like a uniform field, so the cancellation is imperfect and a net force remains.

**Why the force is attraction and never repulsion.** An induced moment is not free to point any way it likes: it is created by the field and therefore always parallel to it. Iron is attracted to **either** pole of a magnet, which is not true of another permanent magnet, where the orientation is fixed in advance and repulsion is possible.

**The everyday observation this explains.** Bring a magnet near an iron needle and the needle first **turns** (torque) and then **jumps** to the magnet (force). Both are seen, which rules out the options offering only one of them. And a needle placed near a magnet but already aligned with the field still moves — torque zero, force not.

rows.stem: A galvanometer shows full scale deflection for a current \(\mathrm{I}_g\). If a shunt of resistance \(\mathrm{S}_1\) is connected to the galvanometer, it gets converted into an ammeter of range \((0 - \mathrm{I})\). When resistance of the shunt is made \(\mathrm{S}_2\), its range becomes \((0 - 2\mathrm{I})\). Then \(\left(\frac{\mathrm{S}_1}{\mathrm{S}_2}\right)\) is
rows.solution:
**The answer is (C): \(\dfrac{2\mathrm{I} - \mathrm{I}_g}{\mathrm{I} - \mathrm{I}_g}\).**

**The shunt relation.** To convert a galvanometer of resistance \(G\) into an ammeter of range \(0\) to \(I\), a shunt \(S\) is placed **in parallel** so that at full scale the galvanometer takes \(I_g\) and the shunt takes the rest, \(I - I_g\). Equal potential differences across the two branches give

\(I_gG = (I - I_g)S \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \boxed{\ S = \dfrac{I_gG}{I - I_g}\ }\)

**Apply it twice.**

\(S_1 = \dfrac{I_gG}{I - I_g} \qquad\text{(range } 0\text{ to } I)\)

\(S_2 = \dfrac{I_gG}{2I - I_g} \qquad\text{(range } 0\text{ to } 2I)\)

**Take the ratio**, and \(I_gG\) — the only part involving the galvanometer itself — cancels:

\(\dfrac{S_1}{S_2} = \dfrac{I_gG}{I - I_g}\times\dfrac{2I - I_g}{I_gG}\)

\(\boxed{\ \dfrac{S_1}{S_2} = \dfrac{2I - I_g}{I - I_g}\ }\)

**The cancellation of \(G\) is the point.** The question gives no value for the galvanometer's resistance, and none is needed — a ratio of two shunts on the **same** instrument cannot depend on it. Spotting that in advance tells you the answer must be built from \(I\) and \(I_g\) alone, which all four options are.

**Is the answer bigger or smaller than 1?** Since \(2I - I_g > I - I_g\), the ratio exceeds \(1\): \(S_1 > S_2\). That makes sense — the **wider** range needs the **smaller** shunt, because more of the total current has to be diverted away from the galvanometer. Options (B) and (D) are both less than \(1\) and can be discarded on this reasoning alone, without algebra.

**Why (A) is wrong in a subtler way.** \(\dfrac{I + I_g}{I - I_g}\) has the right shape and is greater than \(1\), but the numerator carries \(I + I_g\) rather than \(2I - I_g\). It is what comes of writing the second shunt's current as \(I + I_g\) instead of \(2I - I_g\) — that is, of doubling the wrong thing. The range doubles to \(2I\); the galvanometer's full-scale current \(I_g\) is a fixed property of the instrument and does not.

**A sense of the numbers.** A typical galvanometer has \(I_g\) of a few milliamps and \(G\) of tens of ohms, while an ammeter range is amps — so \(I \gg I_g\), the ratio is close to \(2\), and both shunts are a small fraction of an ohm. The shunt also lowers the meter's total resistance, which is exactly what an ammeter needs, since it is connected in series.

rows.stem: A coil of area of cross-section \(0.5\ \mathrm{m}^2\) is placed in a magnetic field acting normally to its plane. The field varies as \(\mathrm{B} = 0.5t^2 + 2t\), where B is in tesla and t in seconds. The emf induced in the coil at t = 1s is
rows.solution:
**The answer is (C): 1.5 V.**

**Set up the flux.** The field is normal to the plane of the coil, so \(\cos\theta = 1\) and

\(\phi = BA = \left(0{\cdot}5t^{2} + 2t\right)\left(0{\cdot}5\right)\)

**Faraday's law.** The area is constant, so only \(B\) varies with time:

\(|\varepsilon| = \left|\dfrac{d\phi}{dt}\right| = A\left|\dfrac{dB}{dt}\right|\)

**Differentiate the field.**

\(\dfrac{dB}{dt} = \dfrac{d}{dt}\left(0{\cdot}5t^{2} + 2t\right) = t + 2\)

**Evaluate at \(t = 1\) s**, and only here — this is the step that has to come **after** the differentiation:

\(\left.\dfrac{dB}{dt}\right|_{t=1} = 1 + 2 = 3\ \mathrm{T\,s^{-1}}\)

\(|\varepsilon| = 0{\cdot}5 \times 3\)

\(\boxed{\ |\varepsilon| = 1{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{V}\ }\)

**The trap the distractors are built on: differentiate FIRST, substitute SECOND.** Putting \(t = 1\) into \(B\) gives \(B = 2{\cdot}5\) T, and it is tempting to do something with that number. But the emf depends on the **rate of change** of the field, not on its value — a field can be enormous and induce nothing at all if it is steady. Option (A), \(0{\cdot}5\) V, is what comes of using only the \(0{\cdot}5t^{2}\) term's coefficient; option (B), \(1{\cdot}0\) V, of using \(A \times 2\), the linear term alone.

**What each term contributes.** The \(2t\) part of the field changes at a constant \(2\) T/s, so on its own it would give a **steady** emf of \(1{\cdot}0\) V. The \(0{\cdot}5t^{2}\) part changes at \(t\) T/s, contributing \(0{\cdot}5t\) volts — zero at \(t = 0\) and growing without limit. At \(t = 1\) they contribute \(1{\cdot}0\) V and \(0{\cdot}5\) V respectively.

**Note that the emf is NOT constant.** \(|\varepsilon| = 0{\cdot}5(t + 2)\) rises steadily with time, which is why the question has to name an instant. At \(t = 0\) it would be \(1{\cdot}0\) V; at \(t = 2\) s, \(2{\cdot}0\) V.

**And the minus sign.** Faraday's law carries one, expressing Lenz's law — the induced current opposes the growth of the flux. The question asks for the emf **induced**, so its magnitude is what is wanted, and all four options are positive.

rows.stem: In a Young's double-slit experiment in air, the fringe width is found to be 0.44 mm. If the entire setup is immersed in water \(\left(n = \frac{4}{3}\right)\), the fringe width will be
rows.solution:
**The answer is (C): 0.33 mm.**

**The fringe width in a Young's experiment.**

\(\beta = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d}\)

Immersing the whole apparatus changes **only \(\lambda\)**. The slit separation \(d\) and the screen distance \(D\) are geometry — unchanged by the water — and the source's **frequency** is unchanged too, since that is fixed by the emitting atoms.

**What the water does to the wavelength.** In a medium of refractive index \(n\), the speed falls to \(c/n\) while the frequency stays put, so

\(\lambda' = \dfrac{\lambda}{n}\)

**The light gets SHORTER wavelengths, so the fringes get NARROWER:**

\(\beta' = \dfrac{\lambda' D}{d} = \dfrac{\beta}{n}\)

**Substituting.**

\(\beta' = \dfrac{0{\cdot}44}{4/3} = 0{\cdot}44 \times \dfrac{3}{4} = 0{\cdot}33\ \mathrm{mm}\)

\(\boxed{\ \beta' = 0{\cdot}33\ \mathrm{mm}\ }\)

**The direction of the change is worth settling before any arithmetic.** Water makes the wavelength shorter; shorter wavelength means a smaller path difference is enough to reach the next maximum; so the fringes crowd **together**. Options (A), \(0{\cdot}88\) mm, and (D), \(0{\cdot}44\) mm, can therefore be eliminated at once — one has the fringes widening, the other unchanged.

**Why option (B), \(0{\cdot}59\) mm, is offered.** It is \(0{\cdot}44 \times 4/3\) — the right factor applied the wrong way up. Dividing rather than multiplying by \(n\) is the whole arithmetic of the question, and getting the *direction* right first is what protects against it.

**Why the FREQUENCY is the thing that does not change.** It is set by the source, and the wave crossing into the water must keep pace with what arrives at the boundary — one crest in, one crest out, or they would pile up. So \(\nu\) is preserved and \(v = \nu\lambda\) forces \(\lambda\) to fall along with the speed. It is the wavelength that is a property of the medium, never the frequency.

**A note on colour.** Since frequency is what the eye responds to, light does **not** change colour on entering water, even though its wavelength there is three-quarters of the value in air. Quoting a colour by its wavelength always means its wavelength in vacuum.

rows.stem: The radius of curvature of a convex mirror is 30 cm. It forms an image of an object which is half the size of the object. Find the separation between the object and the image.
rows.solution:
**Setting up.** For a **convex** mirror with \(R = 30\) cm,

\(f = \dfrac{R}{2} = +15\ \mathrm{cm}\)

positive, because a convex mirror's centre of curvature lies **behind** it.

**What "half the size" tells us.** A convex mirror always forms a **virtual, erect, diminished** image, so the magnification is positive:

\(m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = +\dfrac{1}{2} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad v = -\dfrac{u}{2}\)

**Because the image is known to be erect, the sign of \(m\) is not a guess.** Had the mirror been concave, \(m = \pm\tfrac{1}{2}\) would both be possible and the question would have two answers.

**Apply the mirror formula.**

\(\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}\)

\(\dfrac{1}{-u/2} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{15}\)

\(-\dfrac{2}{u} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{15}\)

\(-\dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{15} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad u = -15\ \mathrm{cm}\)

**and then the image distance:**

\(v = -\dfrac{u}{2} = -\dfrac{-15}{2} = +7{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{cm}\)

**Both signs come out right, which is the check.** \(u = -15\) cm places the object **in front** of the mirror, where a real object must be; \(v = +7{\cdot}5\) cm places the image **behind** it, which is what "virtual" means.

**The separation.**

The object is \(15\) cm in front, the image \(7{\cdot}5\) cm behind, and the mirror lies between them — so the distances **add**:

\(\boxed{\ \text{separation} = 15 + 7{\cdot}5 = 22{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{cm}\ }\)

**Why they add rather than subtract.** Object and image are on **opposite sides** of the mirror. Subtracting \(7{\cdot}5\) from \(15\) would be right only if both lay on the same side, as happens with a concave mirror forming a real image. Sketching the two positions either side of the pole settles it in a moment and is worth the ten seconds.

**A check against the mirror's known behaviour.** The image distance \(7{\cdot}5\) cm is less than \(f = 15\) cm, as it must be: for a convex mirror the virtual image always lies between the pole and the focus, however far away the object is, approaching \(f\) only as the object recedes to infinity. And \(|v| < |u|\), confirming the image is diminished.

rows.stem:
Calculate the energy released/absorbed (in MeV) in the nuclear reaction :

\({}^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H} + {}^{3}_{1}\mathrm{H} \longrightarrow {}^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H} + {}^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H}\)

Given : \(m\left({}^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H}\right) = 1.007825\ \mu\)

\(m\left({}^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H}\right) = 2.014102\ \mu\)

\(m\left({}^{3}_{1}\mathrm{H}\right) = 3.016049\ \mu\)
rows.solution:
**The reaction.**

\({}^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H} + {}^{3}_{1}\mathrm{H} \longrightarrow {}^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H} + {}^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H}\)

*(The masses are printed in the question with the symbol \(\mu\); the unit meant is the **unified atomic mass unit, u**, for which \(1\ \mathrm{u} = 931{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{MeV}/c^{2}\).)*

**Step 1 — total mass of the reactants.**

\(m_R = 1{\cdot}007825 + 3{\cdot}016049 = 4{\cdot}023874\ \mathrm{u}\)

**Step 2 — total mass of the products.** Both are deuterium, so the same mass twice:

\(m_P = 2 \times 2{\cdot}014102 = 4{\cdot}028204\ \mathrm{u}\)

**Step 3 — the mass difference.**

\(\Delta m = m_R - m_P = 4{\cdot}023874 - 4{\cdot}028204 = -0{\cdot}004330\ \mathrm{u}\)

**The sign is the answer to the question.** \(\Delta m\) is **negative**: the products are **heavier** than the reactants. Mass has been created, so energy must have been supplied — the reaction **ABSORBS** energy rather than releasing it.

**Step 4 — convert to energy.**

\(E = |\Delta m| \times 931{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{MeV} = 0{\cdot}004330 \times 931{\cdot}5\)

\(\boxed{\ E = 4{\cdot}03\ \mathrm{MeV\ ABSORBED}\ }\)

**Why this reaction costs energy, and what it says about binding.** Energy is released only when the products are more **tightly bound** than the reactants. Here \({}^{3}\mathrm{H}\) (binding energy \(8{\cdot}48\) MeV) is broken up to make two \({}^{2}\mathrm{H}\) nuclei (\(2{\cdot}22\) MeV each, \(4{\cdot}44\) MeV together), with the free proton contributing none. Going from \(8{\cdot}48\) MeV of binding to \(4{\cdot}44\) MeV loses about \(4{\cdot}04\) MeV — the number just computed, reached independently of the mass arithmetic.

**Where the question is easy to get backwards.** In most nuclear problems \(\Delta m\) comes out positive and energy is released, so the habit is to take the modulus and announce a release. The stem here says "released/absorbed" precisely because the sign is the thing being tested. Always subtract in a fixed order — reactants minus products — and read the sign rather than the size.

**A note on precision.** \(\Delta m\) is the difference of two numbers that agree to four significant figures, so the seven-figure masses are not decoration: rounding them to four figures would destroy \(\Delta m\) completely. This is the general situation in nuclear physics, and it is why atomic masses are tabulated to so many places.

rows.stem: A proton of energy 1.6 MeV approaches a gold nucleus (Z = 79). Find the distance of its closest approach.
rows.solution:
**The physical picture.** The proton is fired head-on at a gold nucleus. Both are positive, so the proton is repelled and slows; at the **distance of closest approach** \(d\) it has stopped momentarily, and all of its kinetic energy has become electrostatic potential energy.

\(K = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{(Ze)(e)}{d}\)

**Rearranging:**

\(\boxed{\ d = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{Ze^{2}}{K}\ }\)

**Substituting**, with \(K = 1{\cdot}6\ \mathrm{MeV} = 1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{6} \times 1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}\):

\(d = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 79 \times \left(1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}\right)^{2}}{1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{6} \times 1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}}\)

**One factor of \(1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}\) cancels top and bottom**, which is the shortcut worth taking:

\(d = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 79 \times 1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}}{1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{6}} = 9 \times 79 \times 10^{9-19-6}\)

\(d = 711 \times 10^{-16}\ \mathrm{m}\)

\(\boxed{\ d = 7{\cdot}11 \times 10^{-14}\ \mathrm{m}\ }\)

**The cancellation seen more generally.** Writing the kinetic energy as \(K = eV\) with \(V = 1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{6}\) volts turns the formula into

\(d = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{Ze}{V}\)

with a single power of \(e\). Expressing an energy in electronvolts and then dividing by \(e\) is the same trick that makes stopping-potential questions one-liners.

**What the number means.** \(7{\cdot}1 \times 10^{-14}\) m is \(71\) femtometres — about **ten times** the radius of a gold nucleus (roughly \(7\) fm). So this proton never reaches the nuclear surface: it is turned back well outside, by the Coulomb repulsion alone, and the **strong** nuclear force never comes into play. That is exactly the regime in which Rutherford's scattering formula holds, and it is why his analysis using only Coulomb's law worked.

**And why the atom is mostly empty.** Compare \(71\) fm with the atomic radius, about \(10^{-10}\) m — some \(1400\) times larger. Even this closest approach happens deep inside the electron cloud, which is why alpha particles sail through gold foil essentially undeflected unless they chance to come this near a nucleus.

**A caution on "head-on".** The formula assumes the proton is aimed straight at the nucleus, so that all its kinetic energy is available. A glancing approach retains some kinetic energy at the turning point, and the closest approach is then larger.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation and the Photon
rows.stem: A photosensitive surface of work function 2.1 eV is irradiated by radiation of wavelength 150 nm. Calculate (i) the threshold wavelength, (ii) energy (in eV) of an incident photon, and (iii) maximum kinetic energy of emitted photoelectron.
rows.solution:
**The constants used**, since the stem supplies none:

\(h = 6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}, \qquad c = 3 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}, \qquad 1\ \mathrm{eV} = 1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}\)

**(i) The threshold wavelength.**

The threshold is the longest wavelength whose photon still carries exactly the work function:

\(\phi_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \lambda_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\phi_0}\)

\(\lambda_0 = \dfrac{6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^{8}}{2{\cdot}1 \times 1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}989 \times 10^{-25}}{3{\cdot}36 \times 10^{-19}}\)

\(\boxed{\ \lambda_0 = 5{\cdot}92 \times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m} = 592\ \mathrm{nm}\ }\)

**The work function must be converted to joules** before dividing — that \(1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}\) in the denominator is the step most often dropped.

**(ii) The energy of an incident photon.**

\(E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^{8}}{150 \times 10^{-9}} = 1{\cdot}326 \times 10^{-18}\ \mathrm{J}\)

Converting to electronvolts:

\(E = \dfrac{1{\cdot}326 \times 10^{-18}}{1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}}\)

\(\boxed{\ E = 8{\cdot}29\ \mathrm{eV}\ }\)

*(The printed scheme's working for this part carries \(150 \times 10^{-19}\) in the denominator where the wavelength is \(150 \times 10^{-9}\) m; its stated answer of \(8{\cdot}29\) eV is nonetheless correct.)*

**(iii) The maximum kinetic energy.**

Einstein's photoelectric equation:

\(K_{\max} = E - \phi_0 = 8{\cdot}29 - 2{\cdot}1\)

\(\boxed{\ K_{\max} = 6{\cdot}19 \approx 6{\cdot}2\ \mathrm{eV}\ }\)

**A quicker route through the whole question.** Using \(hc = 1240\) eV·nm turns every step into a division and needs no joules at all: \(\lambda_0 = 1240/2{\cdot}1 = 590\) nm, \(E = 1240/150 = 8{\cdot}27\) eV, \(K_{\max} = 6{\cdot}17\) eV. The small differences from the answers above are only the rounding of \(hc\) (\(1240\) against \(1242{\cdot}8\) eV·nm), and either set is acceptable.

**Reading the result.** The incident light at \(150\) nm is far into the **ultraviolet**, well short of the \(592\) nm threshold in the yellow-green — so emission is vigorous, and the electrons leave with \(6{\cdot}2\) eV to spare, three times the work function itself. The stopping potential would be \(6{\cdot}2\) V.

**What "maximum" is doing in part (iii).** Only electrons escaping from the very surface give up nothing beyond \(\phi_0\). Those freed deeper lose energy in collisions on the way out, so the emitted electrons span every energy from zero up to \(6{\cdot}2\) eV. The photoelectric equation fixes the **top** of that range, never the typical value.

rows.stem:
(i) Define 'temperature coefficient of resistance' of a metal.

(ii) Show the variation of resistivity of copper with rise in temperature.

(iii) The resistance of a wire is \(10\ \Omega\) at 27 °C. Find its resistance at \(-73\) °C. The temperature coefficient of resistance of the material of the wire is \(1.70 \times 10^{-4}\ °\mathrm{C}^{-1}\).
rows.solution:
**(i) Temperature coefficient of resistance.**

The **temperature coefficient of resistance** \(\alpha\) of a material is the **fractional change in resistance per unit rise in temperature**:

\(\alpha = \dfrac{R_T - R_0}{R_0\left(T - T_0\right)} = \dfrac{1}{R_0}\cdot\dfrac{\Delta R}{\Delta T}\)

Its SI unit is \(\mathrm{K^{-1}}\) (equivalently \(^\circ\mathrm{C}^{-1}\), since the two degrees are the same size). It is **positive** for metals, whose resistance rises with temperature, and **negative** for semiconductors and insulators, whose resistance falls.

**(ii) Resistivity of copper against temperature.**

Plot \(\rho\) on the vertical axis and \(T\) on the horizontal. The curve **rises** with temperature and is very nearly a **straight line** over the ordinary range, following

\(\rho_T = \rho_0\left[1 + \alpha\left(T - T_0\right)\right]\)

Two features distinguish the real curve from a perfect straight line, and both are worth drawing:

At **low temperatures** the graph **bends away** from the straight line and flattens, approaching a small **non-zero residual resistivity** as \(T \to 0\) rather than reaching the origin. That residue comes from impurities and lattice defects, which do not freeze out.

At **high temperatures** the line is straight to a good approximation, because resistivity there is dominated by scattering off lattice vibrations, and their amplitude grows nearly in proportion to \(T\).

**(iii) The resistance at \(-73\ ^\circ\)C.**

\(R_2 = R_1\left[1 + \alpha\left(T_2 - T_1\right)\right]\)

The temperature **falls**, so the change is negative:

\(T_2 - T_1 = -73 - 27 = -100\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\)

\(R_2 = 10\left[1 + \left(1{\cdot}70 \times 10^{-4}\right)\left(-100\right)\right] = 10\left[1 - 0{\cdot}017\right]\)

\(\boxed{\ R_2 = 9{\cdot}83\ \Omega\ }\)

**The sign of \(\Delta T\) is the whole arithmetic.** Cooling a metal **lowers** its resistance, so the answer must come out below \(10\ \Omega\); reading \(\Delta T\) as \(+100\) would give \(10{\cdot}17\ \Omega\), and the error announces itself only if you check the direction.

**A note on the reference temperature.** The formula above measures the change from \(27\ ^\circ\)C, where the resistance is known. It can equally be referred to \(0\ ^\circ\)C, giving

\(R_2 = R_1\cdot\dfrac{1 + \alpha t_2}{1 + \alpha t_1} = 10 \times \dfrac{1 - 0{\cdot}01241}{1 + 0{\cdot}00459} = 9{\cdot}83\ \Omega\)

The two agree to three figures. They are **not** the same expression, but with \(\alpha\Delta T\) of order \(10^{-2}\) the difference between them is of order \(\alpha^{2}\Delta T^{2}\), some \(10^{-4}\) — far below the precision of the data. Over a range of hundreds of degrees the two would visibly part company.

rows.stem:
Name the part of the electromagnetic spectrum which are

(i) stopped by face mask worn by welders.

(ii) used in detectors in Earth satellites.

(iii) used in 'short-wave band' in communication.

Also write the order of wavelengths, in each case.
rows.solution:
**(i) Stopped by the face mask worn by welders.**

**Ultraviolet rays**, of wavelength order \(4 \times 10^{-7}\) m down to \(10^{-9}\) m — that is, about **400 nm to 1 nm**.

*Why.* A welding arc is an intense ultraviolet source. UV photons carry a few electronvolts, enough to break chemical bonds, and they inflame the cornea — the condition welders call *arc eye*. The mask's dark glass absorbs them while passing enough visible light to see by.

**(ii) Used in detectors in Earth satellites.**

**Infrared waves**, of wavelength order \(1\) mm down to \(7 \times 10^{-7}\) m — that is, about **1 mm to 700 nm**.

*Why.* Everything warm radiates in the infrared, so an infrared detector on a satellite sees the ground, the sea and the clouds by their own emission, at night as well as by day. This is the basis of remote sensing: crop health, sea-surface temperature and cloud cover are all read from infrared images.

*(The printed scheme gives this range as "1 nm – 700 nm". That cannot be right — \(1\) nm to \(700\) nm is the **ultraviolet** band, the very one it assigns to part (i) above, and the two answers would then overlap almost completely. The intended figure is \(1\) **mm**, and \(1\ \mathrm{mm}\) to \(700\ \mathrm{nm}\) is the standard infrared range.)*

**(iii) Used in the 'short-wave band' in communication.**

**Radio waves**, of wavelength order greater than \(0{\cdot}1\) m; the short-wave band itself spans roughly **10 m to 100 m** (frequencies of about 3 to 30 MHz).

*Why.* Waves in this band are **reflected by the ionosphere** rather than passing through it, so a signal can be bounced between the ionosphere and the ground and reach far beyond the horizon. That is what made short-wave broadcasting intercontinental long before satellites existed.

**The ordering to keep straight**, since all three parts turn on it:

| Radiation | Wavelength | Photon energy |
|---|---|---|
| Radio | \(> 0{\cdot}1\) m | smallest |
| Infrared | \(1\) mm to \(700\) nm | small |
| Visible | \(700\) to \(400\) nm | a few eV |
| Ultraviolet | \(400\) to \(1\) nm | largest of these |

Wavelength and photon energy run in **opposite** directions, since \(E = hc/\lambda\). That is why the ultraviolet — the shortest of the four — is the one that has to be blocked, while radio waves of enormous wavelength pass through a person harmlessly.
